title: Clean Architecture in .NET: A Practical Guide
excerpt: A hands-on look at structuring .NET projects with Clean Architecture — separating concerns without separating your sanity.

content.text: Clean Architecture is not a new idea. Robert C. Martin formalized it, and the .NET community has been debating its merits ever since. After shipping three production services with it, I've landed on concrete opinions about where it helps and where it gets in the way.

The central promise is independence. Your domain logic shouldn't care whether data comes from SQL Server, Redis, or a flat file. Your API layer shouldn't contain business rules. Testability and replaceability follow directly from those constraints.
The dependency rule: source code dependencies must point only inward, toward higher-level policies.

In practice, this means the Domain project references nothing. Application references only Domain. Infrastructure references Application by implementing its interfaces. The API project wires everything together through the DI container.
The Domain layer holds entities, value objects, and domain events. No framework references, no infrastructure concerns — just the rules of the business, expressed in code.

The Application layer orchestrates domain objects to fulfill use cases. It defines the interfaces that Infrastructure will implement — this inversion is the core of the pattern. Application dictates what it needs; Infrastructure provides it.

The handler knows nothing about SQL Server, Entity Framework, or HTTP. It receives a command, applies domain logic, and persists through an abstraction — trivially testable with a mock repository, no database required.

Clean Architecture earns its overhead in systems that evolve — where you might swap an ORM, add a second delivery channel, or need to test in isolation. For a simple CRUD service with five endpoints and a two-year lifespan, it's overkill. Build boring software when the problem is boring.
